Realism

/REE-uh-liz-uhm/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Realism means the practice of depicting people, things, or situations as they actually are, without idealizing them

Critics praised the unflinching Realism of the novel: the author rendered the factory town, with its cracked sidewalks and tired faces, exactly as it was, refusing to soften a single detail.

Worked Example

Instead of painting the harbor at golden sunset, Elena chose realism, showing the rusted hulls, tangled nets, and oil-streaked water just as she saw them on an ordinary gray morning.

Realism is the practice of depicting things as they actually are, without idealizing them. Elena refuses to prettify the harbor: no glowing sunset, no postcard gloss — just the rust, the tangles, and the gray morning she actually observed.

How Realism Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

verisimilitude

verisimilitude: the appearance of being true to life

authenticity

authenticity: faithfulness to how things really are

naturalism

naturalism: a style that presents life exactly as it is found

Antonyms

idealization

idealization: presenting something as more perfect than it really is

romanticizing

romanticizing: making something seem more beautiful or heroic than it is

How Strong Is It? — candor → realism → hyperrealism

candor vs. realism

candor vs. realism: Candor is honest speech in a single moment; realism is a whole practice of depicting the world without prettying it up.

hyperrealism vs. realism

hyperrealism vs. realism: Hyperrealism pushes further than realism, reproducing every pore and shadow so exactly that the image can look sharper than a photograph.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — real-

Root — real-: 'actual, belonging to things themselves,' from Latin res ('thing') by way of realis

Suffix — -ism

Suffix — -ism: 'practice, doctrine, or style,' from Greek -ismos

Put it together

Put it together: Put together, real + -ism means, at its roots, 'the practice of the actual' — an approach that commits to showing things as they truly are, warts and all.

Use the root in a new word: realpolitik

Use the root in a new word: realpolitik: The ambassador practiced realpolitik, basing every treaty on hard facts about power rather than lofty ideals.
